narr: Let's start with the earliest periods of human history in the region.
First, we have the Paleolithic and Mesolithic periods, which represent the Old and Middle Stone Ages.
A significant development was the Neolithic Revolution, marking humanity's transition from hunting and gathering to agriculture.
Jeitun represents one of the earliest Neolithic sites where agriculture first emerged.
The Kelteminar culture followed, characterized by settled fishing communities in river deltas.
The Hissar culture thrived in the river valleys during the Late Neolithic period.

data.title: Week 3 — History of Uzbek Statehood
data.subtitle: Formation of the Republic of Uzbekistan

narr: Moving forward in time, Week 3 covers approximately 3000 years of statehood in the region.
This spans from the first proto-states of Northern Bactria to the khanates, the Russian conquest, and the formation of the modern republic.
Let's explore the key concepts and periods that shaped Uzbek statehood.

data.heading: The Concept of Statehood
bullets: The history of statehood — the formation of political entities, the transformation of adats and tribal-clan forms into definite legal structures under a specific ruler and system.
Tribal-clan forms — control over a territory with limited regulation; transformation into statehood — the unification of different peoples and tribes on the basis of a more developed legal process.
Statehood on the territory of Uzbekistan developed for about 3000 years; the first sprouts appeared in Khorezm (Khwarazm) after the development of urban construction.
The history of statehood is divided into sovereign and dependent periods; the form of statehood was mostly a monarchy until 1920.
A state — a political entity of society created according to definite rules.

Modern statehood — a way of the political organisation of 'society'; the state — the main agent forming the representation of society; nation-states — the organisation of people and territory into formally comparable sovereign governing units.

narr: Let's begin with understanding the concept of statehood in this historical context.
Statehood represents the evolution from tribal-clan systems to structured political entities with defined legal frameworks.
This transformation involved the unification of different peoples and tribes under more developed legal processes.
In the territory of Uzbekistan, statehood developed over approximately 3000 years, with early forms emerging in Khorezm.
Historically, statehood in the region existed in both sovereign and dependent periods, primarily as monarchies until 1920.
A state can be defined as a political entity created according to specific rules, with modern statehood organizing society into nation-states.

data.heading: The Six Periods of the Ancient Statehood of Turkestan
bullets: 1st period: the development of early state forms in Northern Bactria in the second half of the II millennium BC.
2nd period: the beginning of the I millennium BC — the end of the VI century BC — the formation of the states of Bactria, Sogd and Khorezm.
3rd period: the early V century BC — 329 BC — the control of the Achaemenids.
4th period: the end of the IV century — the end of the II century BC — the coexistence of the Hellenistic states, Khorezm and Kangju (Kangüy).
5th period: the end of the II century BC — the I century AD — the Kushan kingdom.
6th period: the I-III centuries — the development and growth of ancient statehood, its final stage in antiquity.

narr: The ancient statehood of Turkestan can be divided into six distinct periods.
The first period saw the emergence of early state forms in Northern Bactria during the second millennium BCE.
During the second period, from the beginning of the first millennium to the 6th century BCE, the states of Bactria, Sogd, and Khorezm formed.
The third period, from the early 5th century BCE to 329 BCE, was characterized by Achaemenid control over the region.
The fourth period, from the late 4th to the late 2nd century BCE, saw the coexistence of Hellenistic states, Khorezm, and Kangju.
The fifth period, from the late 2nd century BCE to the 1st century CE, witnessed the rise of the Kushan kingdom.
Finally, the sixth period, from the 1st to 3rd centuries CE, marked the development and growth of ancient statehood, representing its final stage in antiquity.

data.heading: The Primary States
bullets: Turkestan — a special historical-geographical and historical-cultural region, where civilisations existed for millennia thanks to two great rivers — the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya.

Bactria: present-day Afghanistan, the south of Uzbekistan and Tajikistan; the capital is Bactra. In the second half of the II millennium BC proto-cities arose here, which later consolidated into the Ancient Bactrian kingdom; in the VI century it was occupied by the Achaemenids, then by Alexander the Great; later — the capital of the Greco-Bactrian kingdom, until the Tocharians came.

Sogd: central Uzbekistan; the capital — present-day Samarkand. In the VI-IV centuries BC — a satrapy of the Achaemenids; in 329 BC it was attacked by Alexander the Great and conquered two years later.

narr: Turkestan represents a unique historical-geographical region where civilizations flourished for millennia thanks to the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers.

Bactria, located in present-day Afghanistan, southern Uzbekistan, and Tajikistan, had its capital at Bactra. Proto-cities emerged here in the second millennium BCE, later forming the Ancient Bactrian kingdom.
Sogd, in central Uzbekistan with Samarkand as its capital, was initially a satrapy of the Achaemenids in the 6th-4th centuries BCE before being conquered by Alexander the Great.
Khorezm developed in the territory of present-day Khorezm and became the center of Great Khorezm by the 7th century BCE.
